edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE
edition.deck: A failed execution in Tennessee prompts scrutiny of death-penalty procedures, while security allegations and economic pressures reshape debates from Europe to the US.
edition.editorialNote: Grouped overlapping reports on Christa Pike, the Flydubai cockpit attack, the Manchester allegation and assaults near Aarhus. Danish-language reporting has been rendered in English, retaining its attributions and uncertainties. Allegations and proposals are identified as such.

content.headline: Tennessee prison chief quits after Christa Pike survives execution attempt
content.shortHeadline: Tennessee prison chief quits after failed execution
content.standfirst: Frank Strada is stepping down as Tennessee orders an independent review of the failed lethal injection. Pike remains critically ill; the governor has paused executions in the state through the end of the year.

image.caption: Emergency vehicles arrive at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution after the execution attempt was halted in Nashville.

sources.originalTitle: Outgoing prison chief in Christa Pike case oversaw five ‘botched’ executions, lawyers say
Tennessee’s top prison official resigning after botched execution of Christa Pike
Christa Pike remains on ventilator after failed execution in Tennessee
Tennessee prison chief to resign after Christa Pike's failed execution
Fængselschef trækker sig efter mislykket henrettelse
Tennessee-fængselschef træder tilbage efter mislykket henrettelse
Kvinde i respirator efter mislykket henrettelse

segments.body: Tennessee’s prisons commissioner, Frank Strada, is resigning after death-row prisoner Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital during an execution attempt on Wednesday. Governor Bill Lee has ordered an independent review and halted executions in the state for the rest of the year. Pike’s lawyers said she remained unconscious and on a ventilator.

perspectives.body: Pike’s lawyers say the attempt was the fifth botched execution overseen by Strada across Tennessee and Arizona since 2022. They point to earlier problems finding veins and question whether Tennessee’s procedures, training and secrecy have been adequately addressed.

segments.title: What remains unknown
segments.body: The state has not explained what went wrong. Pike’s lawyers believe problems with intravenous lines caused the drug to enter her body rather than her bloodstream, and have asked officials to preserve evidence. The Department of Correction has said it followed its protocol; the investigation is expected to examine the procedure.

content.headline: UAE says Flydubai co-pilot used cockpit crash axe in attack
content.shortHeadline: UAE says Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe
content.standfirst: The UAE prosecutor general says the co-pilot attempted a terrorist attack on a Dubai–Tel Aviv flight. Passengers intervened after the plane plunged sharply; investigators have yet to establish the suspect’s motive or whether he had links to others.

image.caption: Captain Smit Machchhar, who was injured in the attack on the flight.

sources.originalTitle: Flydubai co-pilot used crash axe to attack captain, says UAE
Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says
Pilot fortæller for første gang om flyangreb: 'Jeg ville ikke lade andre dø'

segments.body: The UAE prosecutor general says the co-pilot of a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv attacked the captain with a crash axe and attempted a “terrorist attack”. The aircraft plunged more than 5,000 metres before passengers entered the cockpit and helped subdue him. Two reserve pilots landed safely in Saudi Arabia.

segments.title: Questions for investigators
segments.body: The captain, Smit Machchhar, was stabbed but is reported to be recovering. The crash axe is normally kept in the cockpit, so investigators are examining how the attack unfolded and the co-pilot’s background. Media reports have named him as Hamam al-Hammami, but authorities have not officially confirmed his identity or established a motive.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that Oman had previously removed the co-pilot from flight training over concerns about extremist views, citing a report and an official. The account says it remains unclear how he was vetted when Flydubai hired him.

content.headline: Russian strikes hit a second major bridge in Kyiv
content.shortHeadline: Russian strike damages second Kyiv bridge
content.standfirst: A strike damaged the Northern Bridge and injured two people, Kyiv’s mayor says, days after repeated attacks on the Southern Bridge. The attacks have disrupted links across the Dnipro, raising concern the capital could be cut in two.

image.caption: Technicians repair overhead trolleybus power lines on Kyiv’s Northern Bridge.

sources.originalTitle: Russia hits second major bridge in Ukraine's capital Kyiv

segments.body: A Russian strike damaged Kyiv’s Pivnichnyi, or Northern, Bridge on Saturday, injuring two people and damaging the road surface and trolleybus wires, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said. It followed repeated attacks this week on the Pivdennyi, or Southern, Bridge, disrupting road, rail and trolleybus connections across the Dnipro River.

segments.title: Risk to the city’s links
segments.body: The bridges connect the western and eastern parts of the capital, whose roughly three million residents rely heavily on the metro to cross the river. Experts say drones are unlikely to destroy the bridges outright, but repeated attacks could force closures or weaken their structures. Officials have discussed ferries and temporary pontoons as contingency options.

content.headline: Spain housing protests grow after emergency measures fail in parliament
content.shortHeadline: Spain protests grow after housing measures are rejected
content.standfirst: Demonstrators across Spain are demanding tenant protections after lawmakers rejected emergency housing decrees. The country faces a reported shortage of 700,000 homes as rents and house prices climb.

image.caption: A large protest in Spain calls for action on the housing crisis.

sources.originalTitle: 'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis

segments.body: Protests took place in cities across Spain on Saturday after parliament rejected two government housing decrees. The proposals included suspending some evictions, extending rental leases, taxing tourist apartments and restricting purchases by investment funds. A tenants’ group in Madrid estimated its march at 500,000 people, while city officials put attendance at 70,000.

segments.title: A widening affordability crisis
segments.body: The measures followed public anger after an 87-year-old woman was evicted when she could not afford a sharp rent increase. The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes; house prices rose 12.2% in the second quarter of 2026 compared with a year earlier. Clashes between some protesters and police were reported in Valencia, where nine officers were injured and five people arrested, according to RTVE.

content.headline: G7 agrees to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel
content.shortHeadline: G7 to release 100 million barrels of fuel
content.standfirst: The coordinated four-month release is intended to ease supply concerns and price pressure, while G7 members pledge not to restrict energy exports among themselves. The mix of crude and diesel, and the timing of partner-country contributions, remain unclear.

image.caption: G7 leaders have agreed to release oil and diesel reserves.

sources.originalTitle: G7 to release millions of barrels of oil and diesel after Trump threat
Petulant Trump will feel empowered by world’s latest surrender to his demands
Truckers plea for fuel duty bailout as diesel prices hit record high

segments.body: G7 leaders have agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel through the International Energy Agency, beginning immediately and continuing over four months. The plan includes a substantial diesel release within 20 days. The agreement also commits members not to impose export restrictions on energy products between them.

segments.title: Relief may be temporary
segments.body: Diesel is vital to freight and agriculture, so higher prices can feed into the cost of food and other goods. Global benchmark Brent briefly fell below $100 a barrel after the announcement, then rose again. It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks or exactly how quickly; experts warn that using reserves is a short-term buffer, not a fix for constrained supply.

perspectives.body: The UK haulage industry says higher diesel costs are squeezing businesses and may reach supermarket prices. An energy-supply expert cited by the i says reserves can buy companies time, but drawing them down reduces protection against future disruption.

content.headline: New York governor vows to change law after Cornell rape allegations
content.shortHeadline: New York governor vows to close rape-law loophole
content.standfirst: Kathy Hochul says she will seek to change rules that can make prosecution harder when a complainant was voluntarily intoxicated. The Cornell allegations remain disputed, and the men named in the civil suit have not been charged with a crime.

image.caption: Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, where the alleged assault took place.

sources.originalTitle: Guvernør vil lukke smuthul efter omdiskuteret voldtægtssag
Cornell frat house rape accuser 'under siege' online, says lawyer
‘They tried to bury it’: The frat house gang-rape case tearing America apart

segments.body: New York Governor Kathy Hochul says she will work with the state legislature to close a legal loophole that she says can hinder rape prosecutions when an alleged victim voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs. Her announcement follows renewed scrutiny of allegations of a group sexual assault at Cornell University in 2024.

segments.title: Investigation reopened
segments.body: The woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, alleges in a civil lawsuit that seven fraternity members assaulted her while she was unable to consent. The men deny the allegations and have not been criminally charged. State Attorney General Letitia James has taken over the reopened investigation; Hochul said she had lost faith in the county prosecutor’s handling of the case.

perspectives.body: Cornell says it imposed consequential disciplinary measures but cannot disclose individual student records. The i Paper also reports conflicting accounts of what Doe told university police in 2024 and what was later alleged in her civil lawsuit.

content.headline: Russia plans steep rise in defence spending as war costs mount
content.shortHeadline: Russia plans a 27% rise in defence spending
content.standfirst: Draft budget figures reported by Reuters and The New York Times point to record Russian defence spending in 2027. Higher borrowing costs and weaker expected energy revenues could bring tax rises and cuts elsewhere, according to the report.

image.caption: Vladimir Putin as Russia prepares a higher defence budget.

sources.originalTitle: Putin pumper flere milliarder i sin krig og sender regningen til russerne

segments.body: Russia plans to spend 17.1 trillion rubles on defence in 2027, 27% above the figure originally planned, according to internal government documents seen by Reuters and The New York Times and reported by TV 2. The proposed amount would be the highest since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

segments.title: Pressure on public finances
segments.body: The report says Russia’s deficit is expected to grow and government debt to rise above 20% of gross domestic product, a threshold Russian authorities have described as safe. The Kremlin is also planning to expand the active military. Higher borrowing costs and sanctions may constrain its ability to finance the war, while cuts to welfare, education and health and possible tax increases could affect households.

content.headline: Search underway for missing medical plane with six aboard off Massachusetts
content.shortHeadline: Medical plane with six aboard missing off Massachusetts
content.standfirst: US authorities are searching off Nantucket after a medical aircraft travelling from Bermuda to Boston lost contact with flight controllers. The cause of the loss of contact and the occupants’ fate are not yet known.

image.caption: Search teams are looking for the aircraft near Nantucket, off Massachusetts.

sources.originalTitle: Medical plane with 6 on board missing off Massachusetts coast

segments.body: Authorities are searching by air and sea off Nantucket, Massachusetts, for a medical plane carrying six people that went missing early Saturday. The Federal Aviation Administration said it lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 shortly after 1am local time. The aircraft had taken off from Bermuda and was due to land at Boston’s Logan International Airport.

The plane belonged to Latitude Air Ambulances, according to its tail number. The company’s flight operations director said there were two pilots and two Canadian medical staff aboard, along with a patient and a relative. Flight data showed a substantial drop in altitude before communications ended; officials have not announced what caused it.

content.headline: Two men charged over alleged bomb plot targeting Manchester Jewish community
content.shortHeadline: Two charged over alleged Manchester bomb plot
content.standfirst: Prosecutors allege Rahman Salehi and Salam Ahmadyan researched targets including Heaton Park synagogue and the Jewish Museum. Both men deny no charge here: they have been charged with terrorism offences and remanded in custody; the allegations have not been tested at trial.

image.caption: Rahman Salehi and Salam Ahmadyan, who are accused of reconnaissance in Manchester’s Jewish community.

sources.originalTitle: Two Iranian men identified Manchester synagogue as site for alleged bomb plot, court hears
Homemade bomb part of alleged plot on Manchester's Jewish community, court told

segments.body: Two men have appeared in court charged with preparing acts of terrorism or assisting another to do so, in connection with an alleged plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish community. Prosecutors allege Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, carried out reconnaissance at locations including Heaton Park synagogue and the Jewish Museum, and sought instructions for making an explosive device.

segments.title: Case to proceed
segments.body: The men were arrested in Manchester on 20 September, shortly before Yom Kippur. They were remanded in custody and are due to appear at the Old Bailey on 23 October. The court heard that prosecutors allege a third person, believed to be operating from Iran, directed the plan. That account is an allegation; the court has not determined guilt.

content.headline: Tories signal cuts beyond £47bn as Badenoch faces conference tests
content.shortHeadline: Tories signal further cuts beyond £47bn plan
content.standfirst: Leaked remarks by shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith indicate Conservatives have discussed savings across government beyond their existing plan. As Kemi Badenoch prepares for the party conference, senior figures are also divided over welfare, the state pension and the size of the state.

image.caption: Andrew Griffith’s comments point to further Conservative spending cuts.

sources.originalTitle: Tories plan to extend cuts beyond £47bn previously pledged, leak reveals
Kemi Badenoch has cemented her image. Now she wants to put her party back on the big stage
Badenoch returns to Conservative conference much stronger than a year ago
Badenoch wants to save the triple lock. But senior Tories want it gone

segments.body: The Conservatives are seeking savings beyond the £47bn in cuts already announced, according to remarks made last year by shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith and reported by the Guardian. Griffith said ministers had discussed going further and finding savings in “every part of government”. A party spokesperson confirmed the Conservatives want additional reductions, including in welfare and what they describe as wasteful spending.

segments.title: Conference choices
segments.body: Badenoch is expected to make the case for lower taxes and a smaller state at the party’s Birmingham conference. The Guardian reports that her personal standing and the party’s polling have improved, but the Conservatives remain behind Labour and Reform in many polls. Senior Tories have also questioned whether the party can maintain its commitment to the triple lock while meeting other spending priorities.

content.headline: Labour’s proposed PIP reforms prompt fears over cash and support
content.shortHeadline: Disabled people raise concerns over proposed PIP changes
content.standfirst: Ministers are considering voluntary services or equipment in place of some cash payments, alongside wider changes to disability benefits. A claimant and advocacy groups warn that support must not be reduced or made harder to access.

image.caption: Imali Chislett, a PIP claimant from Southampton.

sources.originalTitle: The Labour mutiny Burnham faces over triple lock and welfare reforms
I’m a PIP claimant – here’s how I spend my £780 payment

segments.body: The government is considering whether some Personal Independence Payment claimants could voluntarily receive services or equipment instead of some cash. Disability minister Stephen Timms has said the option would not be compulsory. The proposals are part of a review of PIP, which supports disabled people with additional living costs, and wider plans to change welfare spending.

segments.title: Claimants want choice protected
segments.body: Imali Chislett, a claimant who receives about £780 a month, says her payment helps cover a Motability car, transport, energy and disability-related costs. She worries that promised services may not be available and says cash gives people flexibility. Disability organisations cited by the i Paper also argue that reducing cash could worsen health and poverty outcomes.

perspectives.body: Chislett describes the practical expenses her PIP covers, including her adapted car, travel to hospital and wheelchair repairs. She says any move towards employment support must not mean taking away help from people who cannot work.

content.headline: Diesel hits £2 a litre in UK as hauliers press for tax relief
content.shortHeadline: UK diesel tops £2 a litre as hauliers seek relief
content.standfirst: The record price has led the Road Haulage Association to call for a fuel-duty rebate and a pause to planned increases. G7 reserve releases may ease immediate supply pressure, but experts warn they do not resolve longer-term constraints.

image.caption: Fuel prices at a petrol station in Bristol as UK diesel reaches a record high.

sources.originalTitle: Truckers plea for fuel duty bailout as diesel prices hit record high
G7 to release millions of barrels of oil and diesel after Trump threat

segments.body: The average UK diesel price reached 200.01p a litre, a record, according to RAC figures reported by the i Paper. The Road Haulage Association says operators are paying substantially more to fill their vehicles and is urging the government to pause planned fuel-duty increases and offer a rebate to essential users.

segments.title: Supply relief is not a lasting fix
segments.body: The G7 has agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from reserves and dropped plans for restrictions on energy exports among members. An expert cited by the i says releasing emergency stocks can ease immediate pressure but leaves less protection against future disruption. Hauliers warn higher transport costs could eventually feed into prices on supermarket shelves.

content.headline: London council warns it may need a 150% council tax rise
content.shortHeadline: Hammersmith and Fulham warns of possible 150% tax rise
content.standfirst: Hammersmith and Fulham says a steep rise in its council-tax charge could be needed to balance its budget after a major reduction in central funding. Its report says a Band D household could pay £29.11 more a week in 2027–28 under that scenario.

image.caption: Angela Rayner announced funding rules intended to redirect council money to areas of greater need.

sources.originalTitle: London Labour council warns it may raise council tax by 150%

segments.body: Hammersmith and Fulham council says it may need to raise its own council-tax charge by 150% in 2027–28 to balance its budget under current assumptions. The council’s report estimates the increase would add £29.11 a week for a Band D household, excluding the Greater London Authority precept.

segments.title: Funding dispute
segments.body: The west London authority says its government funding will fall from £150.5m in 2025–26 to £72.4m over four years under the new formula. Ministers say the settlement redirects money to areas with greater need and gives councils flexibility; Hammersmith and Fulham argues the formula does not properly reflect deprivation in the borough. No tax rise has yet been set.

content.headline: Plan to reduce armed escorts for some nuclear waste shipments raises concern
content.shortHeadline: Plan to reduce some nuclear waste escorts raises concern
content.standfirst: The Nuclear Decommissioning Authority says tailoring security for some shipments could save money without weakening protection. Critics question the proposal as officials warn of heightened risks to UK infrastructure.

image.caption: Specialist trains carry nuclear material around the UK; the most dangerous loads are escorted by armed officers.

sources.originalTitle: Nuclear waste armed guards face cuts under cost-saving plan

segments.body: The Nuclear Decommissioning Authority is proposing to remove mandatory armed escorts from some nuclear-waste shipments where it says they would not provide a proportionate security benefit. The proposals cover material including plutonium and enriched uranium. The authority says any changes would be risk-based and made with government and regulators.

segments.title: Security and savings in dispute
segments.body: A former Civil Nuclear Constabulary officer argues that armed guards provide deterrence against theft or misuse of dangerous material. A security expert cited by the i Paper says reducing escorts need not automatically increase risk, but the government must explain clearly which shipments would be affected. The Civil Nuclear Constabulary says changes must not compromise safety.

perspectives.body: The Nuclear Decommissioning Authority says current requirements can be excessive in some transport settings and estimates the proposed changes could cut costs for some shipments by 10–20%. The Civil Nuclear Constabulary stresses that safety and security must not be compromised.

content.headline: Pharmacy closures leave some English patients facing long trips for medicines
content.shortHeadline: Pharmacy closures leave patients facing longer trips
content.standfirst: An analysis found 51 high-street pharmacies closed in England between January and August, including 31 in areas covered by an access-support scheme. Patient groups warn that longer journeys can impede access to medicines and advice.

image.caption: A pharmacy closure has left some patients without a nearby branch.

sources.originalTitle: The worst places to live if you are ill – where trips to chemists take an hour

segments.body: Fifty-one pharmacies in England closed between January and August, according to NHS figures analysed by the National Pharmacy Association. Thirty-one were in areas supported by the Pharmacy Access Scheme, intended to protect access where there is no nearby alternative. Some patients now face lengthy journeys to collect medicines or obtain advice.

segments.title: Funding pressure
segments.body: The analysis says about 9.9 million people have seen their local pharmacy close since 2016. Community Pharmacy England says pharmacies face a funding gap despite a recent government increase. Patient representatives warn that longer trips are especially difficult for people with limited mobility or no access to transport.

content.headline: UK and EU discuss transition periods in food and drink trade deal
content.shortHeadline: UK and EU discuss transition periods for food trade
content.standfirst: Negotiators are discussing time for British businesses to adapt to a possible alignment with EU food-safety rules, after Brussels dropped its opposition to transition periods, the i Paper reports. The wider agreement has not been finalised.

image.caption: UK and EU negotiators are working towards agreements on trade and other issues.

sources.originalTitle: Brexit deal inches closer as EU gives ground to UK on food and drink

segments.body: The UK and EU are negotiating an agreement on animal, plant and health rules intended to make food and drink trade easier. Two EU sources told the i Paper that transition periods are now being discussed, allowing businesses time to adapt rather than facing an immediate change in rules.

Industry representatives have warned that an abrupt switch could cost businesses hundreds of millions of pounds a year. The two sides are aiming to agree a package covering food and drink, youth mobility and carbon markets, but talks remain under way; youth mobility is described as a particularly difficult issue.

content.headline: More than 2,000 approved citizenship applicants left waiting as Danish process暂停
content.shortHeadline: 2,055 Danish citizenship applicants left in limbo
content.standfirst: A parliamentary bill listing 2,055 people who had met the citizenship requirements was paused while an expert group considers screening applicants for anti-democratic views. Those affected say they do not know whether they must reapply or how long they will wait.

image.caption: A graphic describes the 2,055 people whose citizenship applications were paused.

sources.originalTitle: Se, hvem fik næsten statsborgerskab? Muslimer, europæere eller unge født i Danmark

segments.body: A list of 2,055 people who had met the requirements for Danish citizenship was due for final parliamentary approval in January. The process has been put on hold while an expert group examines how applicants could be screened for anti-democratic views, leaving those on the list uncertain about what happens next.

segments.title: Applicants describe uncertainty
segments.body: One in four people on the list had lived in Denmark for at least 20 years, according to DR’s review of public records; 130 were born and raised in the country. Josephine Senyondwa, 22, was born in Denmark and says she is worried about how the pause will affect her. Another applicant, Saeid Ashian, says his family is considering whether they can continue to build a future there.

content.headline: Three teenagers accused of attempted family murder in Kastrup shooting
content.shortHeadline: Three teenagers charged over Kastrup family shooting
content.standfirst: Prosecutors allege that three young men fired 15 shots into a home where two parents and their three children were sleeping. No one was hit; all three defendants deny the charges.

image.caption: Two apartments in Kastrup were hit by gunfire in the March attack.

sources.originalTitle: Teenagere forsøgte at slå familie med tre børn ihjel i Kastrup, lyder anklage

segments.body: Three young men have been charged with attempted murder over a shooting in Kastrup in which 15 shots were fired into a family’s apartment. The parents and their three children were inside but were not hit. Prosecutors allege the attack was carried out for payment; the charge sheet does not say what the alleged motive was.

segments.title: Further allegations
segments.body: Two of the defendants are also accused of involvement in other attempted killings and an arson attack in the Copenhagen area in the days before the shooting. The three have denied the charges. Their trial is due to begin at Copenhagen City Court on 25 January next year.

content.headline: Greenland municipality bans alcohol sales amid safety concerns
content.shortHeadline: Greenland municipality temporarily bans alcohol sales
content.standfirst: Naalakkersuisut has stopped the sale and serving of alcohol in Kujalleq at the municipality’s request, citing children’s welfare and public safety. Authorities have not said how long the measure will remain in force or detailed the incidents behind it.

image.caption: The temporary alcohol-sales ban in Kujalleq has no announced end date.

sources.originalTitle: Alkohol forbydes i grønlandsk kommune for befolkningens sikkerhed

segments.body: The Greenlandic government, Naalakkersuisut, has introduced a temporary ban on selling and serving alcohol in the southern municipality of Kujalleq. The measure began on Friday after a request from the municipal council, which said it was concerned about public safety and children’s welfare.

The government’s announcement refers to serious alcohol-related incidents but does not describe them. Mayor Malene Vahl Rasmussen said the community could no longer accept the negative effects of alcohol use. The ban remains in place until it is formally lifted; no end date has been announced.

content.headline: Police investigate whether two assaults on women near Aarhus are linked
content.shortHeadline: Police examine links between two assaults near Aarhus
content.standfirst: Two women were attacked near Riis Skov months apart, leaving some residents afraid to run after dark. Police say it is too early to know whether the cases are connected and warn residents not to form private patrols.

image.caption: Police say it is too early to determine whether the reported assaults are connected.

sources.originalTitle: Politiet efterforsker, om overfald på unge kvinder ved Risskov kan hænge sammen
Kvinder frygter løbetur efter flere episoder: - Det er virkelig uhyggeligt
Overfald på kvindelige løbere får Jacob til at samle bekymrede naboer til aftenture i skoven

segments.body: East Jutland Police are investigating whether two assaults on women near Riis Skov in Aarhus are connected. A 22-year-old woman was attacked in July; a 24-year-old runner was knocked down and held on 28 September before getting free. Police say it is too early to establish whether the incidents have a link.

segments.title: Police urge residents to report concerns
segments.body: Police say they will increase patrols and ask anyone with information to call 114. Residents have described changing their routes or avoiding runs after dark. Police have strongly advised against private patrol groups, saying they could make people feel less safe and that dealing with suspects is the police’s responsibility.

perspectives.body: A local resident has organised small evening walks with neighbours, saying the group is not a security force. Police nevertheless warn against private patrols and say residents should contact them if they see something suspicious.

content.headline: Home Guard uses major exercise to recruit more active volunteers
content.shortHeadline: Denmark’s Home Guard seeks more active volunteers
content.standfirst: The largest Home Guard exercise since the Cold War is taking place at more than 70 sites in Jutland and Funen. Leaders say tasks are growing and they need more active members, despite a recent rise in recruitment.

image.caption: Home Guard members take part in an exercise at Esbjerg Harbour.

sources.originalTitle: Det strømmer ind med folk til Hjemmeværnet. Men de mangler stadig

segments.body: Denmark’s Home Guard is holding Exercise Blåtand at more than 70 locations in Jutland and Funen. The exercise began on Thursday and ends Sunday; organisers are also using the public-facing activity to encourage new recruits.

The Home Guard says it has gained 1,500 volunteers this year, with recruitment at a level last seen in the 1980s. But many current members are reservists, and leaders say they need more active personnel as the organisation’s responsibilities expand.

content.headline: Poll backs blocking teenagers’ social media overnight, but young people disagree
content.shortHeadline: Most Danes back an overnight social media block for teens
content.standfirst: A poll for Digitalt Ansvar found 62% support blocking 15- to 17-year-olds from social media between midnight and 6am. Some teenagers support the idea; others say young people should decide for themselves.

sources.originalTitle: Opbakning til at lukke unges telefoner ned om natten

segments.body: In a Voxmeter poll for the organisation Digitalt Ansvar, 62% of respondents supported blocking 15- to 17-year-olds from social media between midnight and 6am. The organisation wants Denmark to raise the issue in EU discussions, arguing that notifications and feeds can interfere with young people’s sleep.

segments.title: No decision taken
segments.body: Teenagers interviewed by TV 2 expressed mixed views. Two 17-year-olds called a nighttime restriction reasonable, while another student said young people should be able to manage their own phone use. Education and research minister Christina Egelund said the issue required political responsibility and could be discussed in EU negotiations; no ban has been adopted.

content.headline: Experts warn illegal IPTV services may expose users to cyber risks
content.shortHeadline: Report warns illegal IPTV may pose cyber risks
content.standfirst: A report commissioned by a content-protection group warns that illegal streaming services could expose users’ data and be exploited for cyberattacks or manipulated broadcasts. The report describes potential risks; it says no signal manipulation has yet been documented.

image.caption: Illegal IPTV services offer access to many channels but may carry security risks, according to a new report.

sources.originalTitle: Tusindvis bruger tjenesten – nu advarer eksperter om overhængende risiko

segments.body: A report by cybersecurity researchers commissioned by Nordic Content Protection warns that illegal IPTV services may expose users’ data and internet connections to criminal operators. It says those connections could be resold or used in cyberattacks, and that manipulated copies of broadcasts could potentially spread disinformation.

segments.title: Risks and incentives debated
segments.body: The report’s authors say AI could make it easier to alter content in real time, but they cite no confirmed example of manipulated television signals on these services. A media analyst cited by TV 2 says fragmented, expensive subscriptions may push consumers towards illegal streaming; Nordic Content Protection says cost is no justification for paying criminal providers.

perspectives.body: The report was commissioned by Nordic Content Protection, which works against illegal distribution. TV 2 also includes a media analyst’s criticism that streaming services contribute to piracy when content is fragmented and costly.

content.headline: Study challenges official estimate of Denmark’s cross-border shopping losses
content.shortHeadline: Study says border shopping costs Denmark less than estimated
content.standfirst: Researchers say cross-border purchases of sweets, soft drinks and beer cost the Danish state far less in lost revenue than the tax ministry estimates. The study used shopping patterns during Covid restrictions, when travel across the border was curtailed.

image.caption: Researchers say cross-border shopping has less effect on Danish tax revenue than official estimates suggest.

sources.originalTitle: Studie af danskeres indkøbsvaner tegner nyt billede af grænsehandel

segments.body: A University of Copenhagen study estimates that Denmark lost 415 million kroner in 2019 from cross-border shopping on certain goods, excluding tobacco, compared with the tax ministry’s estimate of 1.16 billion kroner. The researchers examined how much spending shifted to Danish shops during Covid restrictions on cross-border travel.

segments.title: Differences by distance
segments.body: The study found cross-border shopping mattered most for households living within 30 kilometres of the border, while researchers detected no change in spending among households 120 kilometres or more away. The authors say the findings should inform debate over taxes on unhealthy products; they do not recommend a particular tax level.

content.headline: Liz Harris on Grouper’s viral hit, streaming fraud and the solace of Helen
content.shortHeadline: Grouper’s Liz Harris on streaming fraud and the joy of collaboration
content.standfirst: A viral resurgence of an old song brought new listeners—and a fraudulent upload that diverted royalties. Reuniting with dream-pop trio Helen, Harris has also found a restorative counterweight to music-making alone.

image.caption: Liz Harris of Grouper and Helen.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: When Grouper’s “Poison Tree” took off on TikTok, Harris discovered it had been uploaded and registered by someone else, who had already collected about six figures. She and her label were able to shut down the scam and reclaim what she was owed; she says fake tracks remain a recurring drain on independent artists.

segments.title: Making music together
segments.body: Harris describes Helen’s second album, Linda’s Head, as a welcome change from Grouper’s solitary process. Playing with friends helped lift her spirits during medical difficulties, and its brighter, collaborative sound lets another side of her emerge. “I’m not just in the corner crying,” she says.

content.headline: Erasure’s Andy Bell and Vince Clarke on friendship, grief and a changed tour
content.shortHeadline: Erasure on friendship, grief and Vince Clarke’s break from touring
content.standfirst: The duo’s 20th album arrives after they supported each other through bereavement. Clarke will direct the tour remotely, a first for Erasure, while Bell discusses the record’s plea for gentler times and the resurgence of homophobia.

image.caption: Vince Clarke and Andy Bell of Erasure.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s a deep soul connection’: Erasure on how 40 years of friendship got them through grief – and why Vince Clarke has quit touring

segments.body: After Vince Clarke’s wife, Tracy Hurley Martin, died in 2024, Andy Bell supported his longtime bandmate; Bell had lost his own partner in 2012. Clarke says Bell gave him all the love and support he could have wanted. The pair describe their bond as closer than friendship—a “deep soul connection”.

segments.title: A different kind of tour
segments.body: Erasure’s new album, Radio!! Radio!!, is accompanied by an arena tour, but Clarke will not perform onstage. He will work remotely as musical director, with keyboard technician Howard Rider playing the synths. Bell says it will not feel the same without his collaborator beside him.

content.headline: Venom’s Cronos made metal dangerous—and helped give black metal its name
content.shortHeadline: How Venom’s Cronos made metal raw, unruly and influential
content.standfirst: Conrad “Cronos” Lant’s theatrical menace and punk-charged sound helped inspire black metal and later generations of thrash bands. His influence extended far beyond Venom’s modest chart success.

image.caption: Venom frontman Cronos pictured in 1985.

sources.originalTitle: No one could terrify like Cronos, the black metal innovator who reignited rock’s hellraising attitude

segments.body: Venom’s early records rejected polished heavy metal in favour of fast, rough playing, hoarse vocals and confrontational occult imagery. The band’s 1982 album Black Metal lent its name to a subgenre; its raw approach also influenced groups including Slayer, Kreator and Anthrax.

segments.title: A persona with limits
segments.body: Lant’s stage presence was deliberately fearsome, but he did not endorse the violence later associated with some of the Norwegian black-metal scene. He called it a shame that those musicians were known for violence rather than their music. Away from the stage, he enjoyed birdwatching and listened to artists including Joni Mitchell and Kate Bush.

content.headline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul reissue shows a classic album still in flux
content.shortHeadline: A new Rubber Soul box set reveals the Beatles at work
content.standfirst: Outtakes, alternate mixes and recording notes turn the anniversary edition into more than a lavish remaster. The review finds fresh ways to hear an album that helped reshape what pop could be.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: The expanded edition includes the UK and US albums, stereo and mono mixes, two discs of outtakes and a detailed account of the recording sessions. The review’s pleasure lies in hearing songs take shape—not in uncovering one definitive version of Rubber Soul, but in seeing how the band’s choices changed its feel.

segments.title: A pivot in pop
segments.body: The review argues that Rubber Soul marked a turning point: its songwriting and studio detail helped widen pop’s ambitions beyond a collection of singles. The American release, with a different tracklist, also shows how label decisions shaped listeners’ idea of the album. The set makes those competing versions part of the story.

content.headline: Elvis Costello’s My Aim Is True box set traces the making of a songwriter
content.shortHeadline: A Costello box set uncovers the path to My Aim Is True
content.standfirst: The 104-track anniversary set places the 1977 debut alongside demos, earlier songs and live recordings. The review hears not a bolt from the blue, but a young songwriter gradually finding his voice and persona.

sources.originalTitle: My Aim Is True (49th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: The collection’s early demos complicate the story of My Aim Is True as an instant breakthrough. Before the album, Costello had written and performed with Flip City, and these tracks reveal a craftsman drawing on American roots songwriters before punk sharpened his sound and public image.

segments.title: A box with a point of view
segments.body: The reviewer finds the first three discs most revealing, as they chart a gradual shift toward the sharper songwriting associated with Costello’s debut. Later live material is less essential, though a reunion performance with the original album’s backing band provides a warm closing note for dedicated listeners.

content.headline: Lambchop strip back the sound on the searching Punching the Clown
content.shortHeadline: Lambchop find new intimacy on Punching the Clown
content.standfirst: Kurt Wagner’s stories remain unruly and sharply observant, but this time acoustic guitar, banjo and choir replace much of the band’s studio artifice. The review hears an intimate, emotionally direct reinvention.

sources.originalTitle: Punching the Clown

segments.body: On Punching the Clown, Wagner is accompanied by co-writer Andrew Broder on acoustic guitar and Justin Vernon on banjo, with choirs adding a country-gospel warmth. Sparse percussion and occasional interruptions leave room for Wagner’s distinctive turns of phrase, including the generation-spanning story of “The New World Wave”.

The stripped-back setting does not make the writing conventional. The review finds death, decay and political unease alongside Wagner’s characteristic humour, and describes the album as both Lambchop’s most mysterious and its most emotionally direct.

content.headline: Hayley Kiyoko on turning Girls Like Girls into a film about queer joy
content.shortHeadline: Hayley Kiyoko turns Girls Like Girls into a film of queer joy
content.standfirst: The singer’s breakthrough song becomes a feature film shaped by her teenage longing and Asian heritage. Kiyoko says the story’s affirming vision feels especially important amid a hostile political climate for LGBTQ+ people.

image.caption: Hayley Kiyoko, singer and director of Girls Like Girls.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s radical to release a film called Girls Like Girls in this climate’: hitmaker turned director Hayley Kiyoko on sexuality, safety and becoming ‘Lesbian Jesus’

segments.body: Kiyoko says the 2015 song and video helped her feel more confident about her sexuality after listeners shared how strongly they related to it. The feature film expands that story into a coming-of-age romance, which she describes as a love letter to her younger self and a chance to show queer and Asian characters on screen.

segments.title: A different kind of visibility
segments.body: Kiyoko says that, rather than centring violence against queer people, she wants to make art that shows them thriving. The film’s accepting father figure reflects her belief that audiences can use stories to imagine forms of support they may not have experienced in their own lives.

content.headline: Olivia Dean faces a copyright lawsuit over I’ve Seen It
content.shortHeadline: Olivia Dean sued over alleged copying of a Bill Withers song
content.standfirst: The owners of Bill Withers’ catalogue allege that Dean’s track borrowed protected musical elements from “Just the Two of Us”. The complaint names her publisher and record label, but not Dean or her collaborators.

image.caption: Olivia Dean performing at the BRIT Awards in Manchester in 2026.

sources.originalTitle: Olivia Dean accused of plagiarism on her I’ve Seen It track

segments.body: Mattie Music Group alleges that “I’ve Seen It” copied substantial parts of “Just the Two of Us”, including its melody. The lawsuit cites an analysis commissioned from a musicologist and says the defendants continued exploiting the track after written notice. These are claims in a newly filed lawsuit, not a court finding.

segments.title: What the complaint seeks
segments.body: The group is seeking damages and an injunction. Sony Music Publishing, Capitol Records and Kobalt Music Publishing America are named as defendants; the complaint does not name Dean or her two co-writers. The report says representatives for Dean, Capitol and Kobalt did not immediately comment.

content.headline: Brassed Off at 30: Mark Herman on the film’s enduring political force
content.shortHeadline: Brassed Off at 30: why its story still resonates
content.standfirst: Writer-director Mark Herman says the film’s mix of comedy and politics helped it find an audience far beyond its Yorkshire setting. He worries that today’s British industry would struggle to back a similar mid-budget film.

image.caption: Pete Postlethwaite in Brassed Off.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I thought Brassed Off might be popular within a 10 mile radius of Barnsley’: the director of Andy Burnham’s favourite film on its 30-year anniversary

segments.body: Released in 1996, Brassed Off follows a colliery band in a fictional South Yorkshire town as its community faces the loss of the mine. Herman says viewers came for the comedy or the politics and often found an unexpected “bonus” in the other. The film drew on the real Grimethorpe Colliery Band.

segments.title: A film the industry might not make
segments.body: Herman says the story’s staying power comes from its broader subject: people and communities being downtrodden. He is pessimistic about space for mid-budget British films today, saying studios increasingly favour blockbusters or micro-budget productions over the kind of risky project Brassed Off was.

content.headline: Behemoth! review: Pedro Pascal struggles in Tony Gilroy’s muddled drama
content.shortHeadline: Behemoth! has ideas, but its many turns never come together
content.standfirst: A classical-music drama about grief and obsession promises a compelling return to feature filmmaking for Tony Gilroy. The review finds it undone by jarring shifts in tone and a frustratingly distant central performance.

image.caption: Pedro Pascal in Behemoth!.

sources.originalTitle: Behemoth! review - Pedro Pascal classical music drama hits all the wrong notes

segments.body: Pedro Pascal plays Alex, a cello maestro back in Los Angeles and haunted by a past relationship. The story moves between family drama, grief and action, but the review finds that its timeline jumps and subplots leave the film feeling aimless rather than intricately constructed.

segments.title: A difficult centre
segments.body: The review singles out Eva Victor’s performance as a reason to wish she were onscreen more, while finding Pascal’s Alex an insubstantial guide through the story. The film is screening at the New York Film Festival, with releases listed for Australia, the US and UK in December.

content.headline: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall captures a concert as a shared ritual
content.shortHeadline: Paul Thomas Anderson turns Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall show into an
content.standfirst: Filmed on 35mm, the concert film preserves the Geese frontman’s piano performance and the unusual stillness of the audience. The review calls it a sumptuous, unadorned document of a singular night.

image.caption: A still from Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall.

sources.originalTitle: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall review – Paul Thomas Anderson’s sumptuous recording is an immediate classic

segments.body: Paul Thomas Anderson and other camera operators filmed Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall performance, with minimal interruption and few embellishments. The review praises the 75-minute film’s colour and close attention to Winter’s voice, piano and the audience’s concentrated quiet.

segments.title: A film for the already converted
segments.body: The film offers no interviews or narration to bring in unfamiliar viewers, the review notes. For those already drawn to Winter’s voice, however, it recreates the feeling of a concert experienced as a rare communion rather than a conventional show.

content.headline: Bassam Tariq found freedom after the stalled Blade reboot
content.shortHeadline: After Blade stalled, Bassam Tariq made a film on his own terms
content.standfirst: Mahershala Ali plays a devout Muslim and contract killer in Tariq’s Houston-set thriller. The director explains how fight scenes prepared for Marvel’s abandoned Blade project found a new purpose in a more personal story.

image.caption: Director Bassam Tariq at the Toronto Film Festival in September 2026.

sources.originalTitle: How Bassam Tariq pivoted from stalled Blade reboot to new Mahershala Ali thriller: ‘I’m happier I made this movie’

segments.body: Tariq and Ali had worked on Blade before the director left the project in 2022. They carried some of their fight planning into Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, a story about a father whose faith and violence collide as he tries to raise his children.

segments.title: A city and its communities
segments.body: Tariq says the film draws on Houston’s religious communities as places where people find social connection, while examining how faith can also harden into dogmatic division. He says the smaller film gave him room to explore questions of grief, fatherhood and spirituality without the demands of a large franchise.

content.headline: Another Skywalker trilogy risks trapping Star Wars in its family saga
content.shortHeadline: Star Wars should move beyond the Skywalkers
content.standfirst: Reports of a possible trilogy continuing the family story have not been confirmed as greenlit. The argument against returning is familiar but pointed: the franchise’s most intriguing recent corners have often been those that looked beyond the Skywalkers.

image.caption: Daisy Ridley as Rey in The Rise of Skywalker.

sources.originalTitle: A new Skywalker trilogy for Star Wars? Going back to the same family-saga well is a waste of time

segments.body: The report says Lucasfilm has hired Jon Watts to direct the first film in a proposed trilogy written by Simon Kinberg, with Daisy Ridley reportedly considered for a return as Rey. The films have not been greenlit, and details remain limited.

segments.title: A chance to widen the galaxy
segments.body: The article argues that Star Wars has already repeatedly concluded the Skywalker story, and that works such as Rogue One and Andor have been strongest when they explored other parts of the galaxy. The challenge, it suggests, is to make room for new stories rather than resurrecting old characters.

content.headline: Why horror films are pushed into comedy at the Golden Globes
content.shortHeadline: The Golden Globes leave horror with an awkward category choice
content.standfirst: The awards’ drama and musical-or-comedy divisions can leave horror films without a natural home. The article examines why Obsession is being submitted as a comedy despite its bleak, violent story.

image.caption: A still from the horror film Obsession.

sources.originalTitle: Horror films like Obsession are shut out of the Golden Globes – unless they pretend to be comedies

segments.body: Focus Features plans to submit Obsession in the Golden Globes’ musical or comedy categories, according to The Hollywood Reporter. The Guardian argues that the choice reflects the awards’ limited categories, not the film’s tone: its story follows a man whose magical trinket forces a woman to love him.

segments.title: A broader awards problem
segments.body: The article says horror has struggled in both categories: dramas are often treated as more prestigious, while horror can seem out of place among comedies and musicals. A comedy-category nomination could nevertheless help an actor’s campaign, as Demi Moore’s Golden Globe win for The Substance demonstrated.

content.headline: James Dean beyond the rebel image: the vulnerable actor behind the icon
content.shortHeadline: The James Dean performance worth remembering
content.standfirst: A close look at Dean’s work in East of Eden moves past the familiar image of the doomed rebel. Its most revealing moment, the essay argues, is a scene of a son reaching for a father who cannot return his embrace.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: Director Elia Kazan used Dean’s simmering anger during an East of Eden scene, encouraging him to provoke co-star Raymond Massey. The essay traces how the actor’s difficult relationship with his own father informed the role, while distinguishing Dean’s spontaneous intensity from Marlon Brando’s more formally trained technique.

segments.title: The image and the performance
segments.body: Dean died aged 24 after three starring roles, and his death helped cement his image as an embodiment of youthful rebellion. The essay argues that East of Eden’s most affecting moment is less about coolness than vulnerability: Cal throws himself toward his father, who remains rigid.

content.headline: Sense and Sensibility finds modern meaning in Austen’s sisters
content.shortHeadline: Why Sense and Sensibility still speaks to modern life
content.standfirst: Georgia Oakley’s darker new adaptation is uneven, the review says, but the story of sisters balancing restraint and romantic feeling remains strikingly current in an age of precarious futures and constant online self-presentation.

image.caption: Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood in Sense and Sensibility.

sources.originalTitle: Every millennial should read Sense and Sensibility

segments.body: The film follows Elinor, who restrains her feelings, and Marianne, whose romantic idealism clouds her judgement. The review connects their different approaches to modern pressures around oversharing, privacy and the demand to make relationships and work fulfil every personal ambition.

The adaptation is described as darker and gloomier than the 1995 version, with Daisy Edgar-Jones praised for conveying Elinor’s contained grief. The review finds the film imperfect, but argues that Austen’s tension between sense and sensibility remains relevant well beyond Regency romance.

content.headline: Friday Night Lights at 20: the small-town drama that trusted its actors
content.shortHeadline: Why Friday Night Lights still feels trailblazing
content.standfirst: The series brought naturalism and complicated lives to a story about Texas high-school football. Twenty years on, its sense of place, improvised performances and unvarnished portrayal of community pressure still stand out.

image.caption: Kyle Chandler and Connie Britton in Friday Night Lights.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Brave from the beginning’: 20 years of Friday Night Lights – the sports drama that dared to be different

segments.body: Peter Berg encouraged the cast to improvise, filmed with handheld cameras and avoided tightly choreographed blocking. The approach gave scenes a spontaneity that felt unusual for network television, while the characters’ pauses and reactions seemed to belong to the people rather than the script.

segments.title: Beyond the field
segments.body: The series uses football to show the expectations placed on young players and the divisions in a small Texas town. Its setting is deliberately limited—fast food, a bar, a car dealership and the field—while the coach and his wife anchor the story in family and community life.

content.headline: Get Jiro turns food culture into an ultraviolent satire
content.shortHeadline: Get Jiro serves up food obsession with a side of violence
content.standfirst: Anthony Bourdain’s graphic novel becomes an adult animation about chefs wielding power in a dystopian Los Angeles. The review finds a camp, gory satire with a sharp undercurrent about food as class currency.

image.caption: Jiro, the sushi chef at the centre of Get Jiro.

sources.originalTitle: Get Jiro: Anthony Bourdain’s ultraviolent sushi chef makes for wild, pulpy television

segments.body: In Get Jiro, food is one of the few pleasures left outside virtual reality, and master chefs command the power of crime bosses. The taciturn sushi chef Jiro is prepared to kill over diners’ culinary crimes, in a story that pushes restaurant culture and food purism into comic-book excess.

segments.title: The bite beneath the joke
segments.body: The review delights in the animation’s deliberately excessive violence and food jokes, but finds a pointed idea beneath the pulp: access to food can become a marker of class and a means of control. The series is based on a graphic novel co-written by Bourdain and Joel Rose.

content.headline: Lenny Rush finds belonging in The Reluctant Vampire
content.shortHeadline: Lenny Rush leads a vampire comedy about fitting in
content.standfirst: Eric Morecambe’s children’s book becomes a surreal family sitcom, with Rush as a young man who discovers he is not a vampire at all. The actor sees Val’s struggle to belong as a recognisable part of teenage life.

image.caption: Lenny Rush as Val in The Reluctant Vampire.

sources.originalTitle: Fangs a million: Lenny Rush on turning an Eric Morecambe classic into a hilarious vampire comedy

segments.body: Val comes from a family of vampires but lacks their skills and dislikes blood; the story eventually reveals he is human. Rush says the series, adapted by Neil and Rob Gibbons, mixes slapstick with pathos and is written to appeal to adults as well as children.

segments.title: Visibility without a label
segments.body: Rush says he did not enter acting to become a spokesperson for disability. After his Bafta-winning role in Am I Being Unreasonable?, messages from parents told him that seeing him on television had encouraged children with dwarfism. He says he was surprised by the effect of that visibility.

content.headline: Richard E Grant’s Traitors blunder gives the celebrity series a wild start
content.shortHeadline: Richard E Grant’s Traitors mistake sets up a chaotic series
content.standfirst: Grant accidentally revealed he was a Traitor almost as soon as the game began. The review argues that the slip, and the cast’s confusion over what it meant, gave the returning celebrity edition a vivid and unpredictable opening.

image.caption: Richard E Grant and Maya Jama, the initial Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Richard E Grant has already ruined The Celebrity Traitors. It’s brilliant

segments.body: After being chosen as a Traitor, Grant told Joe Lycett plainly that he was one. The review says it was a genuine mistake, leaving fellow Traitor Maya Jama to manage the fallout while the Faithfuls tried to interpret an admission they could scarcely believe.

segments.title: An unpredictable format
segments.body: The review sees the blunder as proof of the show’s appeal: celebrities arrive with established public personas, but the game can still provoke behaviour that feels surprising. The first episode also sets up a recruitment twist, with two Faithfuls asked to plead for a place among the Traitors.

content.headline: Nigella Lawson brings unapologetic pleasure to Bake Off
content.shortHeadline: Nigella Lawson makes Bake Off a celebration of eating
content.standfirst: The new judge’s open enjoyment of the contestants’ baking pushes back against the language of guilt and calorie-counting. The writer finds her presence a welcome alternative to the show’s familiar food anxieties.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson on The Great British Bake Off.

sources.originalTitle: Nigella is dismantling skinny culture one ‘naughty cookie’ at a time

segments.body: Lawson rejects describing food as “naughty” and says people should take their pleasures where they can. The article finds that stance quietly striking on a mainstream baking show, where viewers are often surrounded by messages to restrict what they eat.

The piece contrasts Lawson’s relish with earlier judging language that measured a treat against its calories. Its point is not that one judge can undo broader pressures around body image, but that seeing a woman enjoy food without apology offers a different perspective.

content.headline: Sharon Horgan’s Youth raises questions about who gets to look ordinary
content.shortHeadline: Youth’s beauty standard complicates its everywoman heroine
content.standfirst: The comedy casts Horgan as a pressured middle-aged literary agent, but the writer argues that her glamour makes the “everywoman” harder to recognise. The tension opens a broader critique of women’s appearance on television.

image.caption: Sharon Horgan in Youth.

sources.originalTitle: Sharon Horgan’s Youth has one big problem

segments.body: Horgan created and stars in Youth as Alex, a literary agent pulled between her son, ageing parents and an unsettled career. The writer praises the show’s attention to a woman in her fifties while questioning whether its protagonist can feel like an everywoman when she is so conventionally beautiful.

segments.title: Who gets to be imperfect?
segments.body: The article argues that women on screen face narrower appearance expectations than men, even as television makes room for more complex female characters. Its criticism is directed at the convention, not at Horgan, whose writing it sees as capable of creating less idealised roles.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future has fans asking where the show went wrong
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future after its Disney+ deal
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its Disney+ collaboration, cancelled a planned Christmas special and is seeking a new funding partner. Fans and television voices debate the show’s direction, while its next production remains unresolved.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: The BBC has ended its partnership with Disney+ after the hoped-for global boost did not materialise. A planned Christmas special has been cancelled, and the BBC is seeking a new company to help fund future episodes. No one has yet stepped forward, and the corporation has declined interview requests.

segments.title: A format built to change
segments.body: The article traces the show’s history of regeneration and reinvention, and hears criticism of recent scripts alongside concern about how long the series has been off air. Lifelong fan Frank Skinner says the show does not need huge budgets to tell a good story; its next steps remain unknown.

content.headline: The Split Up gives a British Asian family the centre of a glossy legal drama
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up puts a British Asian family at the centre
content.standfirst: The Manchester-set spin-off follows a family-run divorce law firm, with Ritu Arya leading a predominantly British Asian cast. Its creators explain how the new series keeps the original’s relationship drama while making everyday lives its focus.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: Ritu Arya plays Aria Kishan, a barrister whose plans to inherit her father’s firm are disrupted by family grief and a former romantic partner’s arrival. The six-part series keeps the high-stakes divorce cases and tangled relationships of The Split, but moves the story to Manchester.

segments.title: Everyday lives on screen
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted British Asian characters living ordinary lives, rather than being defined by exceptional circumstances. The show’s executive producer, Abi Morgan, describes it as a chance for a new writing team to build on the original series’ family-centred formula.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day has thrilling combat but little else to sustain it
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day’s combat shines in a repetitive campaign
content.standfirst: The prequel stages the series’ defining alien invasion and offers its best-feeling combat yet. The review finds its repeated routes, intrusive collectibles and limited variety wear out the promise of that return to the beginning.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: E-Day revisits the invasion that shaped the series, with familiar soldiers fighting through a city in collapse. The review praises more fluid movement, weighty weapons and destructible environments, saying the cover-based combat remains the series’ great strength.

segments.title: A long way back
segments.body: The campaign repeatedly sends players through similar areas, with collectibles and side objectives interrupting emotional scenes and exploration sometimes punished by mission boundaries. The review argues that the prequel’s setting becomes a constraint, leaving little development beyond the strong opening hours.

content.headline: Resident Evil film recreates the feeling of playing the games
content.shortHeadline: This Resident Evil film adapts the experience, not the heroes
content.standfirst: Zach Cregger’s adaptation leaves out familiar characters to follow an ordinary courier through escalating danger. The analysis argues that its game-like spaces, scarce ammunition and fragmented clues capture the series’ play experience.

image.caption: Director Zach Cregger with actor Austin Abrams on the set of Resident Evil.

sources.originalTitle: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations

segments.body: Rather than centre on familiar heroes such as Leon or Claire, the film follows courier Bryan Hodukavich through an outbreak, moving from a farmhouse to a tunnel, hospital and sewer. The article notes the game-like rhythm of finding weapons while remaining short on ammunition.

segments.title: The player’s perspective
segments.body: Found recordings, brief exchanges and the uncertainty of whether Bryan will survive echo the games’ way of revealing a world in fragments. The article links this approach to the particular vulnerability that Resident Evil creator Shinji Mikami says makes horror effective.

content.headline: Ace Combat 8 review: a thrilling flight sim that fulfils the Top Gun fantasy
content.shortHeadline: Ace Combat 8 delivers an exhilarating Top Gun fantasy
content.standfirst: The game pairs spectacular dogfights with an unexpectedly affecting story and more expressive cutscenes. The review’s main reservation is that busy skies can make objectives difficult to follow.

image.caption: A fighter jet in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.

sources.originalTitle: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy

segments.body: Ace Combat 8 keeps the series’ arcade flying accessible while offering experienced players more demanding controls. The review praises varied missions, explosive environmental detail and the rush of weaving through missiles as music and radio chatter build around the action.

segments.title: More than spectacle
segments.body: New first-person animated scenes bring wing-mates and their relationships to life, and the review finds the story unexpectedly moving. Its caveat: visual clutter can make it hard to work out which target matters, especially during cockpit-view combat.

content.headline: How children are tricked into handing over Roblox accounts and Robux
content.shortHeadline: The Roblox login scam targeting children
content.standfirst: Phishing pages promise free Robux, then capture children’s passwords and security codes before redirecting them to the real game. Cybersecurity researchers and Roblox offer advice, but recovery of stolen currency is not guaranteed.

image.caption: Roblox advises users not to follow links from unknown senders or websites.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting children

segments.body: Scammers post links in video comments and gaming chats, promising free Robux or creating urgency around a limited offer. The fake login pages can resemble Roblox’s site, collect usernames, passwords and two-factor codes, then send children to the legitimate service without an obvious sign of fraud.

segments.title: How to reduce the risk
segments.body: NordVPN advises children to open Roblox through the official app or website rather than links sent to them, and to treat authentication codes like passwords. Roblox says it has security measures to prevent account theft, but does not guarantee it can restore lost currency or items.

content.headline: A father and son revisit the game that first brought them together
content.shortHeadline: Call of Duty brings a father and son back together
content.standfirst: Playing Modern Warfare 2 with his adult son revives a co-op ritual begun when the boy was five. The personal essay finds joy in the game’s failures, teamwork and a temporary return to carefree time together.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game the father and son play together.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The writer and his 22-year-old son return to two Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 missions they could not finish when the son was five. Years later, their different approaches—one cautious, the other charging ahead—become a source of laughter before they learn to work together.

segments.title: A temporary return
segments.body: The father describes the sessions as a rare break from work and adult responsibilities, and says his son expects to remember them as some of their best times together. They will soon move to different parts of the world, giving the shared play a poignancy beyond the game.

content.headline: The volunteer Pokémon professors who keep tournaments running
content.shortHeadline: Meet the volunteer staff behind competitive Pokémon
content.standfirst: At the world championships, volunteer “professors” referee matches, explain rules and help keep players safe. Their work also means handling difficult calls and upset competitors, often outside the spotlight.

image.caption: Attendees at the 2026 Pokémon World Championships in San Francisco.

sources.originalTitle: Meet the real-life Pokémon professors, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battling

segments.body: Around 300 Pokémon professors helped run the 2026 world championships in San Francisco, according to the Pokémon Company International. Their duties range from technical support and teaching to checking results, enforcing rules and ensuring the venue is safe.

segments.title: Making the call
segments.body: Head judge Gemma Byard says competitors may see only one moment of a disputed ruling, while officials must consider the full account. The article also notes that compensation varies and that the company declined to provide an official explanation of how professors are paid.

content.headline: Why players are rejecting games that hold their hands
content.shortHeadline: Players want blockbuster games to leave room for discovery
content.standfirst: Viral clips mocking Marvel’s Wolverine have revived a debate about games that over-explain objectives. The argument distinguishes difficulty from friction, and asks whether too much guidance strips players of agency.

image.caption: Marvel’s Wolverine, whose guidance prompted debate among players.

sources.originalTitle: Why fans are digging their claws into Wolverine over its patronising gameplay

segments.body: The article describes visual prompts in Wolverine that point out objectives, targets and collectibles, and says players have ridiculed the game for making its guidance feel excessive. It argues that difficulty and friction are different: friction leaves room for players to learn, experiment and act for themselves.

segments.title: The pleasure of figuring it out
segments.body: Examples including Hollow Knight: Silksong and Blue Prince show how games can ask players to work out what to do without making every task punishing. The piece hopes the response to Wolverine reminds publishers that discovery and earned progress are part of what makes games engaging.

content.headline: Can a video-game romance count as cheating? GTA VI prompts debate
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI’s romance system sparks a debate about cheating
content.standfirst: Social media users argue over whether nurturing the game’s couple crosses a relationship boundary. The article takes the concern seriously as a sign of real-world disconnection, while noting that views on virtual romance differ.

image.caption: Lucia and Jason, the couple at the centre of Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

segments.body: GTA VI asks players to build the relationship between protagonists Lucia and Jason through dates, messages and other interactions. Some social media users call that “micro-cheating”; the article notes that the game gives players the same relationship-building role whichever character they play.

segments.title: A real-world insecurity
segments.body: The writer does not consider an in-game romance equivalent to cheating, while recognising that couples set different boundaries. The article suggests the intensity of the debate may reflect loneliness and frustration when people feel their partners invest more care in fictional relationships than real ones.
